description: Dünya gözlem verileri ile derin uzay görev kısıtları arasındaki köprüyü kurmak; gelecekteki Mars yüzey operasyonları için zemin hazırlayan veri odaklı, düşük gecikmeli ve yüksek doğruluklu karar destek araçları geliştirmek.
summary: No single place on Earth matches a Moon base site in every respect, so ranking Earth analogs with one overall "similarity score" hides exactly what mission planners need to know. We built an open, interactive tool that compares 5 Lunar South Pole reference regions (Shackleton rim first) with 40 curated Earth sites (10 well-known analogs used as a diagnostic, 30 candidates) axis by axis: mobility (slope, roughness, relief) and surface (albedo), each with Monte Carlo uncertainty. For every site the app shows where the analogy breaks down (1/6 g, vacuum, radiation, 29.5-day lunar day; thermal scoring is kept non-numeric in v1 due to non-equivalent lunar/Earth definitions), lets the user re-weight the axes for a mission (balanced, rover mobility test, optical surface survey), and recommends a compact portfolio of Earth test sites that together cover the most axes. All numbers come from orbital data (NASA LRO LOLA, NASA MODIS, NASADEM, ESA Copernicus DEM) with their source and resolution attached. This helps agencies and teams choose cheaper, better-justified Earth test sites before sending hardware to the Moon.
details:
What it does. A decision-support tool that answers: "Which Earth sites can we use to test equipment for a permanent base at the lunar south pole, for which purpose, and how sure are we?" Instead of one overall similarity score, it reports a separate score per physical axis - Mobility (mean slope, p90 slope, roughness, relief) and Surface (broadband albedo) - each with a Monte Carlo uncertainty band, and states explicitly which lunar conditions Earth cannot reproduce (1/6 g, vacuum, radiation, the 29.5-day lunar day).

How it works. We compare 5 Moon south-pole reference regions (Shackleton crater rim first) with 40 curated Earth sites (10 literature-documented analogues as a diagnostic, 30 candidates including 14 sites in Türkiye). Every feature is computed with the same definition on both bodies, inside the same 1,000 m analysis radius, in projected metric coordinates: Moon from NASA LRO LOLA 5 m/px DEMs and LOLA 1064 nm albedo; Earth from Copernicus DEM GLO-30 and NASA MODIS MCD43A3 albedo. Every value carries its uncertainty, its source product and its native resolution. Per-axis similarity is exp(-D) of the z-scored distance (a ranking index, not a probability); 200 Monte Carlo draws give a 5-95% interval per score. A mission selector (Balanced 50/50, Rover climbing 67/33, Optical survey 33/67) re-weights the axes, and a portfolio routine finds the smallest set of Earth sites that covers the most axes, listing the axes that remain uncovered and belong in a lab.

Results and creativity. Under the steep Shackleton reference, the top-ranked Turkish candidate (Karapinar Meke, 0.528 [0.41-0.57]) is carried by surface-brightness similarity while ranking #11 on mobility - so the tool separates "which site for which subsystem" instead of declaring one winner. With the flat Faustini reference, known analogues rise in mobility (Svalbard #3, Mauna Loa #5, Haughton #6, Atacama #8), which we report as reference-geometry sensitivity. A +/-10% albedo scaling check preserves the ranking (Spearman rho >= 0.87) in all 5 Moon regions. Our creativity is in honesty and structure: per-axis scoring with visible uncertainty, mission-based re-weighting, the "where the analogy breaks down" card, and a transparent open pipeline.

Factors considered. We suspended the thermal axis in v1 because lunar Diviner polar temperatures (29.5-day cycle, vacuum) and Earth MODIS day-night sampling are not equivalent definitions - we do not invent numbers. Coarse data (MODIS ~1 km) is never presented as resolving a 500 m site; candidates are never claimed as confirmed analogues; every score carries its data source and resolution.

Intended impact and benefits. Cheaper and better-justified analogue test campaigns for lunar hardware (rover wheels, camera exposure, solar panels), a reusable open screening method that agencies and rover teams can extend to Mars and to a global site scan, and - for Türkiye - its first quantitative, evidence-based national test-site inventory.

Tools, languages, software. Python 3.11 (numpy, pandas, geopandas, rasterio, xarray, scipy, scikit-learn, pyarrow, matplotlib), Streamlit + pydeck/plotly analysis app, React + Vite + TypeScript + Leaflet interactive web observatory, pytest and an automated data-contract validator, GitHub Actions (CI + GitHub Pages hosting). No special hardware; all data is free and open.

Source code, data and documentation: https://github.com/tilikumotp/endulus
